division.heading: Request for Particulars, Amendments to Pleadings and Close of Pleadings

operative_text.controlling:
3.62(1)  A party may amend the party’s pleading, including an
amendment to add, remove, substitute or correct the name of a
party, as follows:
(a) before pleadings close, any number of times without the
Court’s permission;
(b) after pleadings close,
(i) for the addition, removal, substitution or correction
of the name of a party, with the Court’s prior
permission in accordance with rule 3.74, or
(ii) for any other amendment, with the Court’s prior
permission in accordance with rule 3.65;
(c) despite clauses (a) and (b), whether or not pleadings have
closed, with the agreement of the parties filed with the
Court.
(2)  An amended pleading must be
(a) filed, and
(b) served on each of the other parties
(i) within 10 days after the date on which it is filed, or
(ii) if the pleading is a statement of claim that has not
already been served, in accordance with Division 3,
Subdivision 2.
(3)  A party may, without the Court’s permission, amend that
party’s pleading before or after pleadings close if that amended
pleading is
(a) a statement of defence in response to an amended
statement of claim, an amended counterclaim or an
amended third party claim, or
(b) a reply to an amended statement of defence, amended
statement of defence to an amended counterclaim, or
amended statement of defence to an amended third party
claim.
(4)  A response pleading referred to in subrule (3) must be
(a) filed, and
(b) served on each of the other parties within 10 days after the
date that the amended pleading referred to in subrule (3) is
served.
(5)  If a party has pleaded in response to a pleading that is
subsequently amended and served on that party and the party does
not file and serve a further response to the amended pleading, the
party is assumed to rely on the party’s unamended pleading in
response to the amended pleading referred to in subrule (3).
(6)  This rule does not apply to amendments to a class proceeding
under the Class Proceedings Act.

BOOK_A.commentary:
*1
Information Note Rule 2.7 [Amendments to pleadings in class proceedings] says that after a certification order is made in a class proceeding, pleadings in a class proceeding may be amended only with the Court's permission. Defined Terms Court, file, party, pleading

Related Provisions 2.7 (amending class proceeding);3.65 (amendment by order);3.67 (close of pleadings);3.74 (changing parties);13.17 (amending other documents). Rule 3.62 lets a party unilaterally amend his or her pleading without anyone else's permission or agreement.It allows that in two circumstances: 1.where the pleadings have not yet closed;in other words, before the deadline for the other

side to file a later pleading answering it: R.3.62(1)(a); 2.within a few days after the opposing side has amended its pleading:R.3.62(3). It is not clear whether, or how much, the new unilateral amendment must be related to the opponent's amendment.

Rule 3.62 allows changes to the parties. Rule 3.62 will not apply after an action is certified as a class action. If the suit is begun by Originating Application (e.g.for judicial review), no Rule closes the

pleadings, and they close when the application is first heard by a judge (even if the judge makes a decision on the merits. Because of R.3.62(3), the court is more receptive to an amendment to the statement of claim necessitated by a plea in the statement of defence, even if the pleadings have been closed for a few months.

The Clerk will often not know when these times expire, and may have to assume that they have not expired, and accept the proffered amendment.Rule 3.62 lets one add a new cause of action closely related to the existing one, especially when it flows from facts in the original statement of claim.But court permission is necessary if some defendants have an arguable limitations defence.

BOOK_B.title: Amending pleading

commentary.text: Rule 3.62 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.62. 1. Admissions In Korte v. Cormie (1996), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 431 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal defined “admissions” and indicated, without deciding, that admissions most likely cannot be made in a statement of claim. However, if admissions can be made in a statement of claim, and if they are true admissions, then they may be removed from the statement of claim only with leave. At p. 436, Madam Justice Hunt, speaking for the court said: The Rules do not define “admission”, but there are a number of Rules dealing with admissions, including RR. 25, 71, 119, 162, 165, 219, 230 and 231. These Rules tend to support the view taken by the respondents, namely, that admissions must be responsive to a statement found in pleadings. For example, R. 119 is to the effect that the silence of a pleading “as to any allegation contained in the previous pleading of the opposite party” shall not be taken to be an admission as to the truth of the allegation. Rule 25 concerns acceptance of service of an admission by the solicitor of a party. Rule 162 deals with “admissions of fact” that have been made upon the pleadings. Rules 230 and 231 set out a process for calling upon a party to admit specific facts… It seems to me that, while these cases concerned statements made in Statements of Claim, the statements which were sought to be withdrawn were of much clearer effect than the words sought to be withdrawn here. I do not find it necessary to decide whether it is ever possible to have an admission in a Statement of Claim, although in the face of the Rules mentioned above I am inclined to the view that it is not. Assuming, however, that it is possible to make an admission in a Statement of Claim, such that leave to withdraw it would be required, in this case I agree with the view of the chambers judge that what was sought to be withdrawn is not an admission but “an allegation in the framing of an action”. It is not so unambiguous as to constitute an admission. Thus, in any event, no leave to amend would be required on this ground. [Pleadings in the action had not yet closed.] 2. Amendments after Pleadings Close In Remington Development Corporation v. Enmax Power Corporation, 2022 ABCA 71, the Court of Appeal set out the test for amending pleadings, and made a specific comment about the difference between “hopeless” and “arguable”. The Court said: [33] Assuming some modest amount of evidence is provided in support, any pleading may be amended no matter how careless or dilatory the party seeking the amendment, subject to four exceptions: (1) the amendment would cause serious prejudice not compensable in costs; (2) the amendment is hopeless; (3) unless permitted by statute the pleading seeks to add a new party or cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; or (4) there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first place: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2014 ABCA 74 at para 25. [34] Attila Dogan posited several things that might make a proposed amendment hopeless. These included amendments which do not disclose a cause of action or where the proposed amendment is so inconsistent with the record that it could fairly be described as hopeless: at para 27. [35] Recently, in Swaleh v Lloyd, 2020 ABCA 18 this Court described the test for determining whether a plea is hopeless at para 13: An amendment to add a pleading should not be granted where the claim is hopeless, such that the pleading would have been struck if originally pled: McCargar v Métis Nation of Alberta Association, 2017 ABQB 692 at para 7, aff’d 2018 ABCA 144. A pleading is hopeless only if it is clear and obvious that there is no triable issue: McCargar at para 19. Hopelessness is met if the claim is barred by statute: see for example, Bouvry Exports Calgary Ltd v ING Insurance Company of Canada, 2008 ABQB 61. [36] In articulating the applicable test, the chambers judge at para 33 said, “I think a proposed amendment is hopeless where it is not ‘arguable’.” … [37] There is a difference between the test enunciated by this Court and that articulated by the chambers judge. “Arguable” implies that there are two possible interpretations or conclusions based upon a set of facts; in other words, there is a triable issue. Hopelessness asks if it is plain and obvious that there is no triable issue. . . . . . [41] The chambers judge did not articulate the correct test when she equated hopelessness with whether something was arguable. … 3. Amendments and Limitation Issues In Kydd v. Abolarin, 2011 ABQB 690, 2011 CarswellAlta 1980, 520 A.R. 250, Justice Macklin had before him an appeal from a Master's decision which had permitted amendments to be made to a Statement of Claim. The proposed defendant contended that the applicable limitation period had expired, and his Lordship, at paragraph 19, discussed the approach the Court should adopt in the face of such a contention: 19 In Dow Chemical Canada Inc v. Nova Chemicals Corporation, 2010 ABQB 524, Wittmann C.J. summarized the options for a Court when an amendment is sought and there is a limitations issue: 1. Determine the limitation period has not expired and allow the amendment. 2. Rule the limitation period has expired and therefore consider s 6 of the Limitations Act which provides for when an amendment can be made beyond the limitation period. 3. Find that because of uncertainty in the evidence, the amendments should be allowed subject to the determination of the limitation issue at trial … (Dow Chemical at para. 64). 4. Amendments after Limitation Period I am satisfied that a Court in Alberta, when considering amendments to statements of claim where intervening limitation periods have accrued to the benefit of the defendant, must determine whether or not the interests of justice warrant such an amendment. It must further determine whether the principles underlying the imposition of the limitation period have been affected, including the question of whether the defendant has been prejudiced by the failure of the plaintiff to include in the statement of claim the amendments sought. The burden of showing such prejudice, as in the renewal and next step cases, rests with the defendant…Dumaine v. Kerry (1988), 87 A.R. 70 at 77 (Q.B.). The prejudice spoken of is not the loss of the statutory defence of a limitation period but rather prejudice related to the merits (e.g., loss of evidence, change in the status quo, etc.). The prejudice suffered may well be the raison d'être of the limitation period. However the existence of the limitation period without more does not necessarily prove that the raison d'être exists in a given case. In Korte v. Cormie (1996), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 431 (C.A.), Hunt J.A., speaking for the Court of Appeal, said at p. 443: I am of the view that if an amendment raises the possibility of a limitation argument, leave of the Court should be required to amend. This is so because the inability to rely upon a limitation argument may work prejudice upon the party against whom the amendment is sought. As such, it is a situation that falls outside the broad language of R. 130. The judge hearing such an application for leave to amend has a number of choices. He or she may agree that the new claim is out of time and thus disallow the amendment; may determine that the sort of special circumstances referred to in [Basarsky v. Quinlan, [1972] S.C.R. 380] exist, and allow the amendment nevertheless; or decide that the limitation argument is of the kind that ought to be determined at trial, upon a factual base. 5. Adding a Counterclaim In Crystal Ridge Fuels Ltd. v. McIntosh, 2013 ABQB 618, 2013 CarswellAlta 2000, 573 A.R. 102, 100 Alta. L.R. (5th) 378, Justice Jones said, at paragraph 17: 17 As noted in Marlborough Ford Sales Ltd v. Ford Motor Co of Canada, 2003 ABQB 298, 13 Alta LR (4th) 336 at para 9, the effect of a counterclaim being conjoined with the statement of defence is that a defendant “must bring an application to amend his or her pleadings to add a counterclaim.” This Court also viewed an application to bring a counterclaim as an amendment to the statement of defence in Deuruneft Deutsche-Russische Mineralol Handelsgesellschaft mbH v. Bullen 2002 ABQB 304, 310 AR 164 at para 26. I conclude that adding a counterclaim engages the procedure under Rule 3.62 and, subsequently, either Rule 3.65 or Rule 3.74. 6. General comment on amendments In MTM Commercial Trust v. Statesman Riverside Quays Ltd., 2022 ABCA 328, 2022 CarswellAlta 2819, Justice Slatter made these observations: [32] The granting or denial of an amendment does not necessarily say anything about the merits of the underlying claim or the relevance of any issues raised. Subject to a very few exceptions, the denial of an amendment also does not create an issue estoppel about the issue in the pleading. For example, pleadings are sometimes disallowed because the limitation period has expired. That sort of ruling might create an issue estoppel, but generally an amendment to a pleading signals that the pleaded issue is to be resolved at trial. [33] In short, an amendment might be denied for many reasons, including that it is unnecessary, includes evidence, or for other reasons. The outcome of the amendment application is rarely conclusive about the evidence that could be entered, what will be argued at trial, or the outcome of the trial. The Merits of the Underlying Pleading [34] The granting or denial of an amendment is not a form of summary judgment. It is true that amendments can be denied if they are “hopeless”, but that is not an invitation to turn an application to amend into an adjudication on issues that are properly dealt with at trial: Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corp, 2020 ABCA 265 at para. 38, 15 Alta LR (7th) 67. That is particularly the case in actions like this, which have been ongoing for over a decade, and which are set to be tried in February. In Kent v. Postmedia Network Inc., 2012 ABQB 559, 2012 CarswellAlta 1526, 548 A.R. 73, Justice Tilleman said, at paragraph 14: 14 As it is written, rule 3.62 places the matter in the judge's hand and the evolving case law suggests a continued tilt in favour of a liberal amendment of pleadings. As long as there is some foundation and unless there is a significant prejudice or an injustice, the order to allow amendments should be freely given11. I am not saying that every amendment should be automatically allowed, because factors such as bad faith, unreasonable delay, or questionable motive are always in play and may prove fatal to the Amendment request …. In paragraph 31 of Kwok v. Canada (Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council), 2013 ABQB 395, 2013 CarswellAlta 1201, Justice Mahoney quoted Justice Tilleman's comment with approval. 7. Pseudonyms In Anglin v. Pankiw, 2022 ABCA 362, 2022 CarswellAlta 3254, the Court of Appeal discussed the use of pseudonyms when the name of a party is not known, and the obligation to amend the pleadings as soon as the identity of the party is ascertained. The Court said: [8] All parties acknowledge the tradition of naming unknown defendants by using the pseudonyms “John Doe” and “Richard Roe”. However … once the plaintiff finds out the real name of the “John Doe” defendant, it is incumbent on him to take timely steps to amend the pleadings to properly name that defendant. A plaintiff is always required to correctly name every defendant. [9] Any required amendment should be made before any other substantive step is taken in the litigation. In exigent circumstances interlocutory relief (such as an injunction or an Anton Piller order) might be obtained against an unknown John Doe defendant before the style of cause is amended: see MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v Simpson 1996 CanLII 165 (SCC), [1996] 2 SCR 1048. However, there is nothing urgent about a noting in default, and in this case the appellant had been identified. Specifically, it would be inappropriate for the plaintiff to attempt to proceed to trial with a known defendant still described as “John Doe”…. [10] Further … the primary obligation is on the plaintiff, not on the unnamed defendant, to move to correct the plaintiff's pleadings. [11] … The use of a pseudonym, however, is not a misnomer. …
